The vector `level[0]` is filled with the single value `1`, representing that student 1 knows the news at time 0. 

While the input still contains pairs `parent child`, the program processes each pair one by one. 
For the current pair it scans all indices `i` from `0` to `students‑1`. 
At each index it checks whether exactly one of the two students of the pair is already stored in `level[i]`. 
If the first student (`parent`) is found in `level[i]` but the second (`child`) is not, the program puts `child` into the next vector `level[i+1]` and stops checking further indices for this pair. 
(If the second student were the one already present, the same test would add the first student to the next level, but the code only adds when the first student is present.)

After all pairs have been read, the program scans the `level` array from the beginning. 
It looks for the first index `i` whose vector is empty. 
When it finds such an index, it prints `i‑1` and stops. 
Thus the printed number is the highest index that contains at least one student, which corresponds to the last “time step” that received a new student.

3. After all neighbours are processed, the pair `u` is removed from the queue and `vizitat[u.node]` is set to 1, marking that student as processed.

Thus each student is processed once, and its neighbours are added to the queue with a distance one greater than the current student’s distance. Because the queue orders by distance, students with smaller distances are processed earlier.

After the loop finishes, the program scans the `d` array to find the largest distance value stored. That maximum value is printed. This value represents the longest number of steps needed for the news to reach any student, starting from student 1.

It builds an adjacency list: an array of lists where the list at index \(i\) contains all students that are friends with student \(i\). 
For example, if the input contains “1 2”, the number 2 is added to the list for 1 and the number 1 is added to the list for 2.

After the graph is built, the program prepares three arrays of length \(N+1\):

* `visited` – marks whether a student has already been taken from the processing queue. 
* `parent` – stores the student that first discovered this student. 
* `d` – stores a value called “depth” that the program calculates for each student.

A linked list called `stack` is used as a queue. The student with id 1 is added first, and its parent is set to –1. 
The program then repeatedly removes the first element from the queue (`pollFirst`). 
When a student `u` is removed, it is marked as visited. 
For every friend `v` of `u` that has not yet been visited, the program:

1. Sets `parent[v]` to `u`. 
2. Computes a depth value for `v` by walking up the parent chain from `u` back to the root (student 1), counting how many steps are taken. 
3. Stores that count in `d[v]`. 
4. Adds `v` to the end of the queue.

Thus each student is processed once, and its neighbours that are not yet processed are queued for later processing. The order in which neighbours are added is the order they appear in the adjacency list, so the queue behaves like a first‑in, first‑out structure.

After the queue becomes empty, every student has a depth value in `d`. 
The program scans all students from 2 to \(N\) and keeps the largest depth found. 
That maximum depth is printed as the final result.

In short, the program builds a graph, walks through it starting from node 1, records a depth value for each node based on how many parent links separate it from the start, and finally outputs the largest depth among all nodes.

After building the graph the program creates several arrays. 
`dist[i]` holds the current best known distance from vertex 1 to vertex i, initially set to a very large number except `dist[1] = 0`. 
`p[i]` stores the predecessor of i on the best path found so far, initially –1.

The main processing loop runs \(n-2\) times. In each iteration it scans all vertices \(u\) from 1 to \(n\). For each vertex it looks at every edge in `adj[u]`. 
If the distance to the neighbour `v` can be improved by going through `u` (i.e., `dist[v] > dist[u] + edge.cost`), the program updates `dist[v]` and records `u` as the predecessor of `v`. 
A boolean flag is set when an improvement occurs, and the inner loop breaks early, moving to the next vertex.

After the repeated relaxation passes, the program performs one more scan of all edges. If any edge still offers a shorter path, it prints `dist[n]` immediately. 
Finally, it prints `dist[n]` again, which is the distance from vertex 1 to vertex n after all relaxations.

Thus the program outputs the length of the shortest path from vertex 1 to vertex n in the given graph.
